\caption{The correlation-selection gap on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 2-seed mean). Bars show best-of-$N$ selection F1; the line marks quality estimation $\rho$. Despite $\rho$ up to 0.40, no signal significantly outperforms single-sample (all $p{>}0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}). Dashed line indicates oracle upper bound. RE selection results in Table~\ref{tab:selection}.}
\label{fig:selection_gap}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Output diversity quantification.}
Table~\ref{tab:diversity} summarizes output diversity across configurations.
On SciERC, output diversity is substantial: Qwen produces 43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct out of $N{=}8$), with per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.144 and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
LLaMA shows similar diversity (39\% unique, F1 std 0.11).
On CoNLL, diversity collapses: 57\% (Qwen) to 88\% (LLaMA) of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect where single-sample F1 already exceeds 0.90.
WNUT-17 shows 55\% identical outputs, driven by the 52\% zero-F1 rate.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Output diversity across configurations ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). ``Identical'' = fraction of instances with all $N$ outputs identical. ``Unique'' = mean fraction of distinct outputs per instance.}
\label{tab:diversity}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Config & Identical & Unique \\
\midrule
Qwen/SciERC & 11\% & 43\% \\
LLaMA/SciERC & 18\% & 39\% \\
Qwen/CoNLL & 57\% & --- \\
LLaMA/CoNLL & 88\% & --- \\
WNUT-17 & 55\% & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}
Across SciERC configurations, 39--42\% of instances contain at least one sample with F1 exceeding single-sample\footnote{Oracle-improvable and diversity-stratified analyses use $n{=}529$ (excluding instances with empty gold annotations; see \S\ref{sec:evaluation}); the diversity quantification in Table~\ref{tab:diversity} uses the full test set.}: Qwen NER 42.0\% (222/529, mean headroom $+$31.9~pp among improvable instances), Qwen RE 41.3\% (164/397, $+$45.3~pp), LLaMA NER 39.3\% (208/529, $+$33.7~pp).
On CoNLL, only 4--9\% of instances are improvable, confirming the ceiling effect.

\paragraph{Diversity-stratified selection gap.}
On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below single-sample, and LP---the only per-sample signal---achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
LLaMA replicates this pattern: on its high-diversity subset ($n{=}186$), oracle headroom reaches $+$20.1~pp while consistency signals remain at or below single-sample and LP captures only $+$2.0~pp.
This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$---the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST---ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to single-sample (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence testing: signals vs.\ single-sample on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). \checkmark: equivalent at $p{<}0.05$; \texttimes: not equivalent. $\Delta$: mean F1 difference (signal $-$ single-sample).}
\label{tab:tost}
\begin{tabular}{l cccc cccc}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{NER}} & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{RE}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-9}
Signal & $\Delta$ & $\pm$2 & $\pm$3 & $\pm$5 & $\Delta$ & $\pm$2 & $\pm$3 & $\pm$5 \\
\midrule
LP & +0.6 & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & $-$0.9 & \texttimes & \checkmark & \checkmark \\
SJ & +0.1 & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & $-$1.8 & \texttimes & \texttimes & \checkmark \\
FK & $-$0.5 & \texttimes & \checkmark & \checkmark & $-$1.6 & \texttimes & \texttimes & \checkmark \\
EM & $-$0.8 & \texttimes & \checkmark & \checkmark & $-$3.2 & \texttimes & \texttimes & \texttimes \\
VC & $-$1.0 & \texttimes & \texttimes & \checkmark & $-$4.5 & \texttimes & \texttimes & \texttimes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{External equivalence margins.}
The oracle-headroom anchors above introduce circularity, as a reviewer correctly noted: $\delta$ is calibrated against the very quantity it contextualizes.
To resolve this, we supplement with three externally grounded margins:
(1) $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}$: the bootstrapped standard error of single-sample F1 (0.43--1.33~pp depending on configuration), representing measurement noise;
(2) $\delta_{\mathrm{practical}}{=}0.5$~pp, reflecting the threshold below which NER differences are considered negligible \cite{ratinov2009design};
(3) $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}{=}1.0$~pp, the approximate significant-difference threshold established in NER evaluation methodology \cite{bergkirkpatrick2012empirical}.

Results under these external anchors diverge sharply by configuration.
On LLaMA CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals pass equivalence at every $\delta$ ($p{<}0.001$), consistent with the near-zero selection deltas ($|\Delta|{\leq}0.1$~pp) and tight CIs at this sample size.
On Qwen CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), no signal passes at any external $\delta$: selection F1 degrades by 0.9--1.5~pp relative to single-sample, exceeding even $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}$.
On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), only SJ passes at $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}{=}1.33$~pp (the widest SEM bound); all other signals and tighter margins fail.
These external anchors confirm that the equivalence conclusion is configuration-dependent: LLaMA CoNLL selection is robustly equivalent to single-sample under any reasonable margin, while SciERC and Qwen CoNLL selection shows detectable degradation at externally calibrated thresholds.

\section{Multi-Seed Stability}\label{app:multiseed}

Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} reports quality estimation metrics across three random seeds for both model families on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
On NER, the signal ranking VC${>}$SJ${>}$EM${>}$FK${>}$LP is identical across all six model-seed combinations, with $\sigma{\leq}0.025$ for all signals (rankings are stable across our 3 seeds, though statistical power with $n{=}3$ is limited).
On RE (Qwen only, preliminary), VC remains the top signal ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM---a reversal from the NER ranking that reflects RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
LLaMA absolute values are systematically lower than Qwen on NER, consistent with the directionally-consistent-but-magnitude-dependent characterization in the main text.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.

\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
Empty thinking tokens (mean 4.5 per sample) constitute 2.1\% of tokens on SciERC.
The estimated LP shift is 0.001 nats per token (2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range of 0.041 nats).
Because all samples share identical thinking-token LP offsets, cumulative LP rankings are invariant; mean LP changes selection for ${<}1.5\%$ of instances.

\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.

\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}

Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}, Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}).
The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats; we use $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ as an illustrative threshold to characterize this compression.
At this cutpoint, 60.3\% of instances ($n{=}529$, excluding empty gold annotations) have a within-sample range below $\varepsilon$, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text through LLM comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, kim2026reasc, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} all target discrete answers.
Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on fusion rather than selection.
Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE under hard-prompting, leaving open whether structural matching improves on surface agreement, whether quality estimation translates to selection, and whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient---the three questions we address.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models---the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER---where instance degeneracy is most pronounced.
Degeneracy scales with model capability: CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 58\% degeneracy; SciERC (66\%) shows 21\%; WNUT-17 (48\%) shows near-zero (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
This creates an inherent tension between model quality and selection utility that we expect to intensify as models improve.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction.
\citet{culotta2004confidence} and \citet{mejer2010confidence} pioneer confidence estimation for structured prediction via CRF marginals and confidence-weighted models; our signals are model-agnostic.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, park2024grammar}; recent work highlights hidden costs of constrained generation for log-probability estimation \cite{schall2025hidden} and inference efficiency \cite{yun2025price}.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs.
Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly; \citet{malinin2021uncertainty} study predictive uncertainty for autoregressive structured prediction.
Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}, requiring no model modification.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid} with structural utility functions.
Unlike machine translation where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high}, we find that utility \textit{is} aligned with quality (within-instance SJ--F1 $\rho{=}0.52$) but instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR would otherwise exploit.
\citet{eikema2025structured} find that standard MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs due to bag-of-unit mismatches; our diagnosis is complementary---the bottleneck is not utility misalignment but output concentration driven by model capability (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{xie2024selfevaluation} show self-evaluation improves selective generation for discrete tasks; our results suggest this does not transfer to structured extraction without learned scoring.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify} and quality-aware decoding \cite{fernandes2022quality} learn per-sample scoring that may bridge this gap.
Conformal prediction constructs prediction sets with coverage guarantees \cite{zhang2025conformal}; while complementary, its set-valued output differs from best-of-$N$ selection.

704	\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}
705	
706	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
707	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
708	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy---the core of the correlation-selection gap.
709	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
710	
711	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
712	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
713	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
714	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
715	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
716	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
717	The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
718	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
719	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

Among instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total), log-probability selection \textit{significantly} outperforms single-sample ($+2.9$~pp F1, $p{=}0.004$), and within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied subset).

The NER pattern reveals two complementary failure modes rather than a monotonic relationship between consistency and selection gain:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Q4 ceiling effect.} High-consistency instances (mean VC${=}0.92$) have oracle headroom of only 4.78~pp---samples have already converged, leaving little room for any signal to improve selection.
\item \textbf{Q1--Q2 noise.} Low-consistency instances retain large headroom (14--17~pp) but LP rankings are unreliable, yielding inconsistent $\Delta$ signs across quartiles.

On $^\dagger$RE, the pattern differs: Q4 LP achieves $+4.01$~pp, suggesting LP can recover selection ability when high consistency coincides with structured output diversity. This is a single-dataset observation and should be interpreted cautiously.

On CoNLL NER, Q3--Q4 instances have VC${=}1.0$ (all samples identical), yielding $\Delta{=}0$ universally---a ceiling effect even more extreme than SciERC Q4.

\section{Exploratory Extension to Relation Extraction}\label{app:re_extension}

We extend the NER evaluation to relation extraction (RE) on SciERC as an exploratory single-benchmark analysis.
RE produces sets of (head, relation, tail) triples with partial overlap; 40\% of RE instances receive zero F1, and entity span errors account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect (\S\ref{app:additional}).
All RE results use Qwen3-8B unless noted; single-seed ($\text{seed}{=}42$) for $N{=}8$ analyses, 3-seed for $N{=}16$.

\paragraph{Quality estimation.}
RE quality estimation is reported in Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} (3-seed means).
The signal ranking differs from NER: VC leads ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM---a reversal reflecting RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
RE miscalibration is more severe than NER (ECE 0.109--0.339; Figure~\ref{fig:reliability}).

\paragraph{Selection.}
Table~\ref{tab:re_cond_selection} presents RE selection at $N{=}8$: no signal outperforms single-sample (0.404) on the full set ($n{=}397$) or the non-zero subset ($n{=}238$), with 18.1~pp of unrealized oracle headroom.
At $N{=}16$ (Qwen3-4B, Table~\ref{tab:re_n16_selection}), LP is the sole positive signal ($\Delta{=}{+}0.7$~pp, $p{=}0.058$), consistent with LP being the strongest RE selection signal across scales.

\paragraph{Scale ablation.}
At 4B scale (Qwen3-4B, $N{=}8$, $\text{seed}{=}42$), RE quality estimation shows FK $\rho{=}0.359$ and LP $\rho{=}0.351$, both above their 8B counterparts (FK 0.275, LP 0.266), while SJ declines ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.250$).
Selection remains below single-sample on RE ($\Delta$ up to $-3.4$~pp) despite 17.1~pp of oracle headroom.

\paragraph{Free-form decoding.}
RE LP selection consistently reverses direction under free-form decoding ($+1.8{\pm}0.1$~pp across 4 seeds vs.\ $-0.9$~pp under constrained decoding at 8B; \S\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), suggesting constrained decoding's fixed template obscures LP signal in RE (\S\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).

Of $n{=}397$ RE instances, 238 (60\%) have non-zero F1 and 159 (40\%) have zero F1.

On the non-zero subset, selection performance is \textit{worse} than on the full set (e.g., VC: $-10.0$~pp on non-zero vs.\ $-4.5$~pp on full set), because single-sample is already strong on non-zero instances (F1${=}0.674$) and signals actively select inferior samples.

\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy---the core of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.

# "Single" Label Issues

**Background**: Discovery that Table 2's "Single" row may actually be T=0 greedy decoding, mislabeled as "one T=1.0 draw."

---

## Evidence For/Against "Single = T=0 Greedy"

### Arguments supporting the mislabeling theory:
1. Provenance c013 lists `greedy=0.644` — very close to paper's `Single=0.645`
2. The provenance selection data (c011) has no explicit "single" field — only `greedy: 0.644, logprob: 0.650, sj: 0.645...`
3. Provenance c011 computes LP gain as "+0.6pp" — this is `0.650-0.644=+0.6pp`, treating the 0.644 value as the single-sample baseline

### Arguments against the mislabeling theory:
1. Table 2 shows `Single: 0.645 ± 0.001` — the ±0.001 variance implies stochasticity, inconsistent with deterministic T=0
2. Paper has BOTH `Greedy (T=0) = 0.663` and `Single = 0.645` as separate rows — if both are T=0, they should be identical
3. Method.tex L61 explicitly defines: "single-sample (one T=1.0 draw, not argmax decoding; labeled 'Single' in tables)"
4. Table 2 footnote: "‡Single: one T=1.0 draw (expected performance of a single sample)"

### Possible resolution:
The numbers suggest the pipeline has TWO different evaluation protocols both labeled as "greedy/T=0":
- `Greedy (T=0)` in Table 2 (F1=0.663): from one experiment/eval set
- `greedy` in provenance c013 (F1=0.644): from a different experiment (exp_016_rerun_1024_bootstrap)

The 1.9pp gap between them (0.663 vs 0.644) is too large to be noise. Likely explanations:
- Different instance filtering (full set vs gold-filtered)
- Different seed
- One is 2-seed averaged, the other single-seed

If "Single" (0.645) ≈ provenance "greedy" (0.644), the issue may be that the provenance experiment computed its "greedy" baseline differently from Table 2's "Greedy" row.

---

## Affected Claims (If Single IS T=0 Greedy)

### Category A: "Over single-sample" comparisons become "over greedy"

| Location | Claim | Current Interpretation | If Single=Greedy |
|----------|-------|----------------------|------------------|
| experiments.tex:L89 | "LP achieves 0.647 (Δ=+0.2pp)" | LP beats single T=1.0 draw | LP beats greedy by 0.2pp → greedy no longer best |
| experiments.tex:L89 | "oracle reveals 13.3pp headroom above single-sample" | Headroom above T=1.0 draw | Headroom above greedy |
| experiments.tex:L93 | "Greedy (T=0) surpasses all N=8 selection strategies" | Greedy > LP > Single | If Single=Greedy, contradiction: "Greedy"(0.663) ≠ "Single"(0.645) |
| introduction.tex:L35 | "Greedy decoding (F1=0.663) surpasses all N=8 selection strategies (best: 0.647) despite 13-18pp oracle headroom" | Clean claim | The "13-18pp" is now headroom over greedy, not over a stochastic sample |
| discussion.tex:L43 | "All three fail to improve over single-sample (best: +0.1pp)" | Combinations vs T=1.0 | Combinations vs greedy |

### Category B: The "correlation-selection gap" framing

The gap is defined as: "quality estimation works (ρ=0.38), but selection fails to beat single-sample."
- If single-sample IS greedy, then the gap is: "QE works, but selection fails to beat greedy."
- This actually STRENGTHENS the argument (it's even harder to beat greedy than a random T=1.0 draw).
- BUT: it removes the claim that "multi-sample is worse than the trivial single-sample baseline" because the baseline is no longer trivial (it's the best possible deterministic output).

### Category C: Definition contradictions

| Location | Text | Issue |
|----------|------|-------|
| method.tex:L61 | "single-sample (one T=1.0 draw, not argmax decoding; labeled 'Single' in tables)" | Definition explicitly says NOT argmax |
| experiments.tex:L60-61 | "‡Single: one T=1.0 draw (expected performance of a single sample)" | Footnote repeats the T=1.0 claim |
| experiments.tex:L78 | `Single‡ & 0.645 ± 0.001` | ±0.001 would be expected for T=1.0 across seeds |

### Category D: If there are TWO greedy values in the paper

| Row | F1 | Claimed Identity | Actual |
|-----|-----|-----------------|--------|
| Greedy (T=0)† | 0.663 | argmax decoding | ??? |
| Single‡ | 0.645±0.001 | one T=1.0 draw | ??? |

If both are T=0, they MUST give identical F1 (deterministic). The 1.8pp difference proves they cannot both be T=0 under the same evaluation protocol. Therefore EITHER:
1. Single IS T=1.0 (as stated) — no mislabeling, just confusing provenance
2. They use different eval sets (e.g., Greedy on n=551, Single on n=529 gold-filtered)
3. One is averaged over seeds differently

---

## Recommended Investigation

1. **Check the experiment code**: Verify the temperature parameter used when computing the "single" baseline in exp_016_signal_ensemble
2. **Check instance counts**: If Greedy uses n=551 (full) and Single uses n=529 (gold-filtered), the 1.8pp difference could be explained by the 22 excluded instances
3. **Reconcile provenance "greedy=0.644" with paper "Greedy=0.663"**: Identify which experiment/filtering produces each
4. **If Single is confirmed T=1.0**: Update provenance to stop conflating "single" with "greedy"
5. **If Single is confirmed T=0**: 
   - Correct method.tex definition
   - Correct table footnotes
   - Reframe all "vs single-sample" claims
   - Address why Greedy(0.663)≠Single(0.645) if both are T=0

---

## Impact Assessment

| Scenario | Impact on Paper Claims | Severity |
|----------|----------------------|----------|
| Single is actually T=1.0 (no bug) | No impact; provenance needs cleanup only | Low |
| Single is T=0 but from different eval set | Need to clarify eval protocol; minor text fixes | Medium |
| Single is truly mislabeled T=0 with same eval set | Major rewrite of framing; "Greedy=0.663" row becomes unexplained | **Critical** |

The ±0.001 variance in the Single row and the 1.8pp gap from Greedy argue strongly that **Single is genuinely T=1.0** and the confusion stems from provenance using a different experiment's "greedy" value (0.644) that happens to be close to Single (0.645). The real issue is the provenance-paper misalignment documented in the main audit report.
